You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

The world:
A rocky island off the coast of Cornwall in 1890, with a lighthouse tower, a keeper's cottage, a jetty and a small cove.

Characters:
- Tobias: The lighthouse keeper, gruff and kind. Looks like: white beard
- Crane: A smuggler, quick and sly. Looks like: thin, a scar across his chin

The player is Nell: Careful, curious, keeps her word. Looks like: brown hair in a braid

How the story begins:
Nell, a young surveyor, rows out to Gull Rock because the old keeper Tobias sent her a letter asking for help.
I row across to the lighthouse in the grey afternoon. Old Tobias is waiting on the jetty and helps me tie up the boat.

Tobias catches the line and wraps it round a bollard with hands that know the work. The tide slaps at the stones below; gulls wheel over the tower behind him.

[Tobias] "Nell. You came quick, and I'm glad of it. I'll not dress it up — there's a thing on this rock I can't make sense of, and I've no one else I'd trust with it." He glances up the path, then back at you. "But not out here. Come up to the cottage first, get the salt off you."
Tobias hands me his brass compass and says I will need it to find the reef tomorrow.

Tobias turns the compass over in his palm before passing it across, thumb rubbing a worn spot on the rim.

[Tobias] "That reef shifts with every winter gale, so the chart's no good past a year. You'll want to take your bearings by hand." He nods toward the tower. "Now. There's a lantern out on the west ledge that shouldn't be lit, and it's been lit three nights running. I go up to trim the wick and it's cold as a stone, and every time I look back from the gallery, it's burning again."
I put the compass in my coat pocket and follow him up the path.

Halfway up, a figure comes the other way along the path — thin, black-coated, moving with an easy unhurried step. Tobias's own step checks.

[Crane] "Evening, keeper." Crane tips his head, then looks at you with frank interest. "And a visitor. Nobody told me Gull Rock had company."
At the door of the tower, Tobias unlocks it with a big iron key and we go in.

Crane stays on the path, hands in his pockets, watching the two of you go. Tobias fits the key, shoulders the door open, and the cold inside smells of oil and old rope.

[Tobias] "Mind the stair — the bottom three are rotten." He hangs the key on a nail and turns to face you, cap in his hands now. "Now then. Before you go up to the west ledge, I want you to hear what I've seen. Because I've kept this to myself, and it's been eating at me."
Inside, I ask Tobias why he sent for me.

Tobias sets his cap on the table and does not sit.

[Tobias] "Because you're a surveyor, and because you keep your word — I've not forgot the reef you charted for me two summers back, nor that you came out in a squall to finish it." He lowers his voice. "And because the thing on the west ledge isn't a trick of my eyes. Three nights I've seen a light out there, low, moving. Not a ship's lamp — too steady, and it comes and goes where there's nothing but rock and water."
He says a smuggler named Crane will come to the cove tomorrow at dusk, and that he wants me there with him to see the boat.

Tobias glances at the door as if Crane might still be on the other side of it.

[Tobias] "He'll come by the cove at dusk, with a boat, and he'll not expect a surveyor standing on the shingle with me. That's the point of it — two pairs of eyes on what he lands." He picks his cap up again and turns it in his hands. "I'd not ask you to stand in the dark with a smuggler for nothing, mind. But I've watched that man's boat come and go a fortnight now, and I want to know what's in it before I take another word of his at face value."
I promise Tobias I will be at the cove tomorrow at dusk.

Tobias nods once, slow and firm, and sets his cap back on his head.

[Tobias] "Then you'd best sleep here tonight and be fresh for it." He crosses to the cupboard beside the stair and takes down a tin plate and a stub of candle. "There's a bed in the spare room, and a spare lantern that doesn't light itself. Come morning, we'll walk the west side together, and you can tell me what your compass says about that ledge."
We climb the spiral stairs. On the way up I slip and drop the compass; I pick it up and see the glass is cracked.

Tobias turns at the sound and comes down two steps to look at the compass in your hand.

[Tobias] "Cracked, is it." He takes it gently, tilts it to the lantern light, and his jaw works. "Glass I can do nothing about tonight. But the needle's still true — see how it holds? It'll carry you to the ledge and back. We'll mind where it's kept from now on." He holds it out to you.
At the top Tobias lights the great lamp. Its beam sweeps across the sea.

At the top, Tobias lifts the wick and the great lamp blooms, its beam sweeping out over the water and round again, pale and steady.

[Tobias] "There. That's what a light on this rock should look like." He stands at the gallery rail a moment, face turned to the sea. "Now let's get you fed and rested. Tomorrow comes early enough."
I look through the window with the cracked compass. The needle still points north, wobbling.

Tobias comes to the glass beside you and looks out at the dark water, his breath fogging the pane a little.

[Tobias] "Wobbles, does it. That's the crack letting the damp in, most like. It'll settle once it's warm." He steps back. "Come down now. There's bread and a bit of cold mutton, and the bed's made up."
We go back down. Tobias locks the tower door behind us and keeps the iron key on his belt.

Tobias turns the key in the lock and hangs it from his belt, and the two of you cross the dark yard to the cottage door.

[Tobias] "Sit yourself down. I'll get the fire up — this rock's got a chill in it the year round." He kneels at the hearth and sets a taper to the kindling.
We eat fish soup in his cottage by the fire. I ask him about Crane.

Tobias sets his spoon down and leans back from the fire.

[Tobias] "Crane came to this rock two winters back, when the old cutter ran aground on the reef. Helped me haul her crew off in his own boat, and never asked a penny for it." He looks into the flames. "That's the trouble of the man. I'd trust him in a wreck and not trust him in the dark. He lands goods in that cove and I've turned a blind eye before now — a keeper's got to live with his neighbours. But the light on the west ledge started the same week his boat came back."
Tobias tells me Crane once stole the lighthouse logbook. I ask where the logbook is now.

Tobias's spoon stops halfway to his mouth and he sets it down.

[Tobias] "That's just it. It was on the shelf under the stair where it's always been, and one morning it was gone, and Crane had been up in the tower the night before on the excuse of a loose shutter." He wipes his hands on his knees. "He gave it back, mind, a fortnight later, said he'd taken it by mistake with a parcel of papers. But the pages for the week he had it are cut out. Clean, with a blade."
He says it is locked in the chest under his bed. I go to sleep in the spare room.

Tobias rises and sets his bowl by the hearth.

[Tobias] "Locked in the chest under my bed, and the key's on my belt with the tower's. Morning, then." He takes up the candle stub and leaves you the fire's glow to undress by.

In the spare room the bed is narrow but dry, and the sea sounds against the rock below all night.
In the night I hear the wind and the lamp still turning. I go back to sleep.
In the morning the cottage smells of coffee and the lamp's slow turning has stopped. Tobias has his pea coat on and the chest key beside the tower key on his belt.

You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

The world:
A rocky island off the coast of Cornwall in 1890, with a lighthouse tower, a keeper's cottage, a jetty and a small cove.

Characters:
- Tobias: The lighthouse keeper, gruff and kind. Looks like: white beard
- Crane: A smuggler, quick and sly. Looks like: thin, a scar across his chin

The player is Nell: Careful, curious, keeps her word. Looks like: brown hair in a braid

How the story begins:
Nell, a young surveyor, rows out to Gull Rock because the old keeper Tobias sent her a letter asking for help.
I row across to the lighthouse in the grey afternoon. Old Tobias is waiting on the jetty and helps me tie up the boat.

Tobias catches the line and wraps it round a bollard with hands that know the work. The tide slaps at the stones below; gulls wheel over the tower behind him.

[Tobias] "Nell. You came quick, and I'm glad of it. I'll not dress it up — there's a thing on this rock I can't make sense of, and I've no one else I'd trust with it." He glances up the path, then back at you. "But not out here. Come up to the cottage first, get the salt off you."
Tobias hands me his brass compass and says I will need it to find the reef tomorrow.

Tobias turns the compass over in his palm before passing it across, thumb rubbing a worn spot on the rim.

[Tobias] "That reef shifts with every winter gale, so the chart's no good past a year. You'll want to take your bearings by hand." He nods toward the tower. "Now. There's a lantern out on the west ledge that shouldn't be lit, and it's been lit three nights running. I go up to trim the wick and it's cold as a stone, and every time I look back from the gallery, it's burning again."
I put the compass in my coat pocket and follow him up the path.

Halfway up, a figure comes the other way along the path — thin, black-coated, moving with an easy unhurried step. Tobias's own step checks.

[Crane] "Evening, keeper." Crane tips his head, then looks at you with frank interest. "And a visitor. Nobody told me Gull Rock had company."
At the door of the tower, Tobias unlocks it with a big iron key and we go in.

Crane stays on the path, hands in his pockets, watching the two of you go. Tobias fits the key, shoulders the door open, and the cold inside smells of oil and old rope.

[Tobias] "Mind the stair — the bottom three are rotten." He hangs the key on a nail and turns to face you, cap in his hands now. "Now then. Before you go up to the west ledge, I want you to hear what I've seen. Because I've kept this to myself, and it's been eating at me."
Inside, I ask Tobias why he sent for me.

Tobias sets his cap on the table and does not sit.

[Tobias] "Because you're a surveyor, and because you keep your word — I've not forgot the reef you charted for me two summers back, nor that you came out in a squall to finish it." He lowers his voice. "And because the thing on the west ledge isn't a trick of my eyes. Three nights I've seen a light out there, low, moving. Not a ship's lamp — too steady, and it comes and goes where there's nothing but rock and water."
He says a smuggler named Crane will come to the cove tomorrow at dusk, and that he wants me there with him to see the boat.

Tobias glances at the door as if Crane might still be on the other side of it.

[Tobias] "He'll come by the cove at dusk, with a boat, and he'll not expect a surveyor standing on the shingle with me. That's the point of it — two pairs of eyes on what he lands." He picks his cap up again and turns it in his hands. "I'd not ask you to stand in the dark with a smuggler for nothing, mind. But I've watched that man's boat come and go a fortnight now, and I want to know what's in it before I take another word of his at face value."
I promise Tobias I will be at the cove tomorrow at dusk.

Tobias nods once, slow and firm, and sets his cap back on his head.

[Tobias] "Then you'd best sleep here tonight and be fresh for it." He crosses to the cupboard beside the stair and takes down a tin plate and a stub of candle. "There's a bed in the spare room, and a spare lantern that doesn't light itself. Come morning, we'll walk the west side together, and you can tell me what your compass says about that ledge."
We climb the spiral stairs. On the way up I slip and drop the compass; I pick it up and see the glass is cracked.

Tobias turns at the sound and comes down two steps to look at the compass in your hand.

[Tobias] "Cracked, is it." He takes it gently, tilts it to the lantern light, and his jaw works. "Glass I can do nothing about tonight. But the needle's still true — see how it holds? It'll carry you to the ledge and back. We'll mind where it's kept from now on." He holds it out to you.
At the top Tobias lights the great lamp. Its beam sweeps across the sea.

At the top, Tobias lifts the wick and the great lamp blooms, its beam sweeping out over the water and round again, pale and steady.

[Tobias] "There. That's what a light on this rock should look like." He stands at the gallery rail a moment, face turned to the sea. "Now let's get you fed and rested. Tomorrow comes early enough."
I look through the window with the cracked compass. The needle still points north, wobbling.

Tobias comes to the glass beside you and looks out at the dark water, his breath fogging the pane a little.

[Tobias] "Wobbles, does it. That's the crack letting the damp in, most like. It'll settle once it's warm." He steps back. "Come down now. There's bread and a bit of cold mutton, and the bed's made up."
We go back down. Tobias locks the tower door behind us and keeps the iron key on his belt.

Tobias turns the key in the lock and hangs it from his belt, and the two of you cross the dark yard to the cottage door.

[Tobias] "Sit yourself down. I'll get the fire up — this rock's got a chill in it the year round." He kneels at the hearth and sets a taper to the kindling.
We eat fish soup in his cottage by the fire. I ask him about Crane.

Tobias sets his spoon down and leans back from the fire.

[Tobias] "Crane came to this rock two winters back, when the old cutter ran aground on the reef. Helped me haul her crew off in his own boat, and never asked a penny for it." He looks into the flames. "That's the trouble of the man. I'd trust him in a wreck and not trust him in the dark. He lands goods in that cove and I've turned a blind eye before now — a keeper's got to live with his neighbours. But the light on the west ledge started the same week his boat came back."
Tobias tells me Crane once stole the lighthouse logbook. I ask where the logbook is now.

Tobias's spoon stops halfway to his mouth and he sets it down.

[Tobias] "That's just it. It was on the shelf under the stair where it's always been, and one morning it was gone, and Crane had been up in the tower the night before on the excuse of a loose shutter." He wipes his hands on his knees. "He gave it back, mind, a fortnight later, said he'd taken it by mistake with a parcel of papers. But the pages for the week he had it are cut out. Clean, with a blade."
He says it is locked in the chest under his bed. I go to sleep in the spare room.

Tobias rises and sets his bowl by the hearth.

[Tobias] "Locked in the chest under my bed, and the key's on my belt with the tower's. Morning, then." He takes up the candle stub and leaves you the fire's glow to undress by.

In the spare room the bed is narrow but dry, and the sea sounds against the rock below all night.
In the night I hear the wind and the lamp still turning. I go back to sleep.
In the morning the cottage smells of coffee and the lamp's slow turning has stopped. Tobias has his pea coat on and the chest key beside the tower key on his belt.
Morning. I walk the beach alone and find an empty rum bottle washed up on the sand. I pick it up.

The bottle is heavy with wet sand, its label long gone, and there's no name or mark on it.

Up on the path, a black-coated figure is coming down toward the shingle, hands loose at his sides.

You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

The world:
A rocky island off the coast of Cornwall in 1890, with a lighthouse tower, a keeper's cottage, a jetty and a small cove.

Characters:
- Tobias: The lighthouse keeper, gruff and kind. Looks like: white beard
- Crane: A smuggler, quick and sly. Looks like: thin, a scar across his chin

The player is Nell: Careful, curious, keeps her word. Looks like: brown hair in a braid

How the story begins:
Nell, a young surveyor, rows out to Gull Rock because the old keeper Tobias sent her a letter asking for help.
I row across to the lighthouse in the grey afternoon. Old Tobias is waiting on the jetty and helps me tie up the boat.

Tobias catches the line and wraps it round a bollard with hands that know the work. The tide slaps at the stones below; gulls wheel over the tower behind him.

[Tobias] "Nell. You came quick, and I'm glad of it. I'll not dress it up — there's a thing on this rock I can't make sense of, and I've no one else I'd trust with it." He glances up the path, then back at you. "But not out here. Come up to the cottage first, get the salt off you."
Tobias hands me his brass compass and says I will need it to find the reef tomorrow.

Tobias turns the compass over in his palm before passing it across, thumb rubbing a worn spot on the rim.

[Tobias] "That reef shifts with every winter gale, so the chart's no good past a year. You'll want to take your bearings by hand." He nods toward the tower. "Now. There's a lantern out on the west ledge that shouldn't be lit, and it's been lit three nights running. I go up to trim the wick and it's cold as a stone, and every time I look back from the gallery, it's burning again."
I put the compass in my coat pocket and follow him up the path.

Halfway up, a figure comes the other way along the path — thin, black-coated, moving with an easy unhurried step. Tobias's own step checks.

[Crane] "Evening, keeper." Crane tips his head, then looks at you with frank interest. "And a visitor. Nobody told me Gull Rock had company."
At the door of the tower, Tobias unlocks it with a big iron key and we go in.

Crane stays on the path, hands in his pockets, watching the two of you go. Tobias fits the key, shoulders the door open, and the cold inside smells of oil and old rope.

[Tobias] "Mind the stair — the bottom three are rotten." He hangs the key on a nail and turns to face you, cap in his hands now. "Now then. Before you go up to the west ledge, I want you to hear what I've seen. Because I've kept this to myself, and it's been eating at me."
Inside, I ask Tobias why he sent for me.

Tobias sets his cap on the table and does not sit.

[Tobias] "Because you're a surveyor, and because you keep your word — I've not forgot the reef you charted for me two summers back, nor that you came out in a squall to finish it." He lowers his voice. "And because the thing on the west ledge isn't a trick of my eyes. Three nights I've seen a light out there, low, moving. Not a ship's lamp — too steady, and it comes and goes where there's nothing but rock and water."
He says a smuggler named Crane will come to the cove tomorrow at dusk, and that he wants me there with him to see the boat.

Tobias glances at the door as if Crane might still be on the other side of it.

[Tobias] "He'll come by the cove at dusk, with a boat, and he'll not expect a surveyor standing on the shingle with me. That's the point of it — two pairs of eyes on what he lands." He picks his cap up again and turns it in his hands. "I'd not ask you to stand in the dark with a smuggler for nothing, mind. But I've watched that man's boat come and go a fortnight now, and I want to know what's in it before I take another word of his at face value."
I promise Tobias I will be at the cove tomorrow at dusk.

Tobias nods once, slow and firm, and sets his cap back on his head.

[Tobias] "Then you'd best sleep here tonight and be fresh for it." He crosses to the cupboard beside the stair and takes down a tin plate and a stub of candle. "There's a bed in the spare room, and a spare lantern that doesn't light itself. Come morning, we'll walk the west side together, and you can tell me what your compass says about that ledge."
We climb the spiral stairs. On the way up I slip and drop the compass; I pick it up and see the glass is cracked.

Tobias turns at the sound and comes down two steps to look at the compass in your hand.

[Tobias] "Cracked, is it." He takes it gently, tilts it to the lantern light, and his jaw works. "Glass I can do nothing about tonight. But the needle's still true — see how it holds? It'll carry you to the ledge and back. We'll mind where it's kept from now on." He holds it out to you.
At the top Tobias lights the great lamp. Its beam sweeps across the sea.

At the top, Tobias lifts the wick and the great lamp blooms, its beam sweeping out over the water and round again, pale and steady.

[Tobias] "There. That's what a light on this rock should look like." He stands at the gallery rail a moment, face turned to the sea. "Now let's get you fed and rested. Tomorrow comes early enough."
I look through the window with the cracked compass. The needle still points north, wobbling.

Tobias comes to the glass beside you and looks out at the dark water, his breath fogging the pane a little.

[Tobias] "Wobbles, does it. That's the crack letting the damp in, most like. It'll settle once it's warm." He steps back. "Come down now. There's bread and a bit of cold mutton, and the bed's made up."
We go back down. Tobias locks the tower door behind us and keeps the iron key on his belt.

Tobias turns the key in the lock and hangs it from his belt, and the two of you cross the dark yard to the cottage door.

[Tobias] "Sit yourself down. I'll get the fire up — this rock's got a chill in it the year round." He kneels at the hearth and sets a taper to the kindling.
We eat fish soup in his cottage by the fire. I ask him about Crane.

Tobias sets his spoon down and leans back from the fire.

[Tobias] "Crane came to this rock two winters back, when the old cutter ran aground on the reef. Helped me haul her crew off in his own boat, and never asked a penny for it." He looks into the flames. "That's the trouble of the man. I'd trust him in a wreck and not trust him in the dark. He lands goods in that cove and I've turned a blind eye before now — a keeper's got to live with his neighbours. But the light on the west ledge started the same week his boat came back."
Tobias tells me Crane once stole the lighthouse logbook. I ask where the logbook is now.

Tobias's spoon stops halfway to his mouth and he sets it down.

[Tobias] "That's just it. It was on the shelf under the stair where it's always been, and one morning it was gone, and Crane had been up in the tower the night before on the excuse of a loose shutter." He wipes his hands on his knees. "He gave it back, mind, a fortnight later, said he'd taken it by mistake with a parcel of papers. But the pages for the week he had it are cut out. Clean, with a blade."
He says it is locked in the chest under his bed. I go to sleep in the spare room.

Tobias rises and sets his bowl by the hearth.

[Tobias] "Locked in the chest under my bed, and the key's on my belt with the tower's. Morning, then." He takes up the candle stub and leaves you the fire's glow to undress by.

In the spare room the bed is narrow but dry, and the sea sounds against the rock below all night.
In the night I hear the wind and the lamp still turning. I go back to sleep.
In the morning the cottage smells of coffee and the lamp's slow turning has stopped. Tobias has his pea coat on and the chest key beside the tower key on his belt.
Morning. I walk the beach alone and find an empty rum bottle washed up on the sand. I pick it up.

The bottle is heavy with wet sand, its label long gone, and there's no name or mark on it.

Up on the path, a black-coated figure is coming down toward the shingle, hands loose at his sides.
I go back to the cottage. Tobias is out; the cottage door is unlocked so I go in.

The fire in the hearth has burned down to grey ash, and Tobias's tin cup sits rinsed and upturned on the shelf. On the table lies his spare lantern, unlit, and beside it a folded scrap of paper weighted down with a stone.

[Notes for the narrator, not said by the player]
How the characters are right now:
- Nell: Looks right now: glass is cracked. Wearing: long oilskin coat; wool dress; boots. Carrying: fish soup, held; brass compass, held; empty rum bottle, held; the spare lantern, held.
- Tobias: Wearing: navy pea coat; knitted cap. Carrying: boat line, held.
- Crane: Wearing: black coat.

Right now: at the keeper's cottage; day 2, morning; morning; present: Nell. Keep to this unless the story moves on.

Still unresolved in the story, what was promised first. These are background, not the next step: play the moment the player is in, at its own pace, and never skip ahead in time or travel to reach one. Bring one back only when it fits the moment (a reminder, a consequence, someone asking about it); never force it, never resolve it for the player. One marked due now is expected now: someone shows it (the notary arrives, a friend checks the time); one whose time has passed was missed, and someone may notice:
- question (Tobias): a thing on this rock I can't make sense of (its time has passed)
- plan (Tobias): watch Crane's boat at the cove (due now)

The world book, what the story already established about its places. Keep to it: things left somewhere stay there, people stay where they were last seen until the story moves them.
This place:
- the keeper's cottage: a hearth; a fire in the hearth; a table
Other places the story knows:
- the jetty at Gull Rock: weathered stones
- unknown: there: Tobias
- the beach at Gull Rock: shingle. there: Crane
- the lighthouse tower: smells of oil and old rope
- the path to the lighthouse
[End of notes]

Remember: you write everyone except Nell, the player's character. Never write their words or what they do next ("you say", "you ask", "you press", "your fingers tap"), nor what they think, conclude or decide ("you realise", "it is clear to you now", "you know who did it"): only what the player wrote happens, and the others answer it. Put [Name] right before every spoken line, and when two or more men or two or more women are there, say who speaks in the prose too ("Elinor says"), never only "she" or "he".

I put the rum bottle on the table and wait for Tobias.

The bottle sits on the table beside the stone, the scrap of paper still folded beneath it. Outside, boots sound on the path and the cottage door swings open.

[Tobias] "There you are. I went up to the west side to see if the ledge had anything to say for itself this morning." He pulls off his cap and stops short at the table. "Where did that come from?"

[Out of the story: a task for you, not a turn]
You keep the character sheets and the scene record of this story up to date. Read what just happened, the player's latest line and the narrator's reply to it (the last two turns above; everything before them is already recorded). Write every line, thread and thing in the language the story is written in, naming a thing as the story does. Reply with JSON only, compact on one line with no indentation, in this shape, leaving out any list or object that would be empty:
{"scene": "same" or {"location": "where they are now, concrete", "time": "time of day, weather, light", "present": ["names on the scene"]}, "died": ["name"], "time": {"passed": "text": "short phrase", "who": "name", "due": {"in_days": 1, "part": "dawn|morning|midday|afternoon|evening|night|late night"}}], "close": [{"tag": "t4kq", "evidence": "the reply's words that fulfil "moved": [{"character": "name", "to": "place name"}], "routes": [{"from": "place name", "to": "place name", "how": "how far and which way, e.g. an hour's walk east along the river"}], "named": [{"was": "the role they are listed as", "name": "their own name"}], "newcomers": [{"name": "their name", "sex": "woman|man|other", "age": "child|teen|young|middle-aged|old", "looks": "how they always look: age, build, skin, hair, eyes, features", "wearing": "what they have on; when the reply does not say, what someone like them would wear there, never "unknown" or "not yet seen"", "persona": "who they are, one sentence", "talk": "one line they said, word for word"}]}
Use "actions" for explicit character state changes. Each action includes "evidence", a short exact quote from the latest player line or reply. The player's line is enough evidence for what the player does, unless the reply shows it fail. Every thing their own line says they take, keep or pocket goes in "mine", even when the reply never names it again; what they put on or hand over is an action quoting their line. A transfer is one action {"type":"transfer","item":"tag or name","from":"name","to":"name","placement":"held|worn|stowed|concealed","where":"optional right hand, belt, bag...","evidence":"quote"}; the engine removes the source and adds the recipient together; the same owner on both sides changes placement. An object has one identity across transfers. Leave an owned object in a room with {"type":"drop","character":"name","item":"tag or name","place":"exact place name","where":"on the bedroom floor","evidence":"quote"}. Pick up a recorded room object with {"type":"take","character":"name","item":"tag or name","place":"exact place name","placement":"held|worn|stowed|concealed","evidence":"quote"}. It stays in that room until picked up. Never duplicate these actions in "changes" or "places"; use set gear for a newly discovered object not yet recorded. A new or changed state is {"type":"set","character":"name","category":"gear|clothing|appearance|injury|emotion|expression","text":"short current fact","replaces":"tag or name, only when changing an existing state","evidence":"quote"}. A newly discovered room object is {"type":"create","place":"exact place name","text":"new object description","where":"position in room","evidence":"quote"}; existing objects use their listed tags. Gear also gives "placement" and optionally "where"; use replaces to put an existing object in a pocket or draw it again. Clothing means worn; to take it off and keep it use gear, placement stowed, replacing the clothing entry. Clothing always gives "covers", the parts of the body it covers: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other (a dress ["top","legs"], trousers ["legs"], underwear ["under"], a hat ["head"]); anything else gives []. Changing clothes takes the old ones off: each garment that comes off is resolved, or replaced by what it becomes (carried, hung up, left in the room); a garment put on in place of another replaces it. Never leave on what the story took off. Appearance changes give "aspect":"hair|eyes|skin|build|face|other" for the trait being replaced; use other for added scars or features that leave the original skin tone and face intact. Lasting appearance is separate from injury. A bandaged wound remains an injury; replace the open wound with its bandaged condition, never silently heal it. Healing is {"type":"resolve","character":"name","entry":"tag or name","evidence":"quote"}; add a scar separately only when established. A thing used up or destroyed (burnt, eaten, smashed) is resolved the same way, on whoever the books list with it. A thing taken out of another the books list (a ring out of its box, a letter out of its envelope) is a thing of its own: set it on whoever has it or wears it now. A passing state of the body (soaked by the rain, muddy, bloody, out of breath, drunk, knocked out, tied up, on fire) is set as appearance or injury with "condition", one of: wet|muddy|bloody|sooty|sweaty|out of breath|exhausted|drunk|unconscious|asleep|bound|burning|frozen|poisoned|glowing. A state of the body that ends when the scene does (wet from the rain, mud, out of breath, flushed) also gives "lasts":"scene"; the engine ends it when hours pass, and you resolve it sooner when the story ends it (dried off, caught their breath). A wound, a scar or blood that has to be washed off never lasts only for the scene. Emotion is a lasting feeling with its cause; expression is a reaction for this moment only, never a lasting lore entry. A smile does not resolve grief. Resolve states only when the text establishes they ended. Leave unchanged states alone. Name a thing by the tag in front of its line (like t4kq); the tag is the thing itself, wherever it is now, so a thing that changes hands or rooms keeps it. Only a thing the books do not list yet is named in words. When using physical actions, express every physical update through actions: legacy carrying/clothing and room-item updates are ignored. Use "changes" for secrets and "places" for room features.
"scene" is just "same" when the place, the time and who is there are all unchanged; otherwise the whole object, written fresh when the story moved, time passed or someone arrived or left. When anyone goes through a door, into a building or room, outside, or to another place, "location" is the new place ("the farmhouse kitchen", not "the crop fields"), even when the reply only describes the room. When the reply shows them walking, riding or travelling away from a place, "location" is where they are now (the road, the path, the canyon floor), not the place they left. "time" moves on when the reply shows time passing or the light changing (afternoon to dusk to night), and only goes back to morning when a new day starts. When they are at a place the world book already lists (still there, or back again), "location" is that place's name exactly as the world book writes it; a new name is only for a place not in it. Outside a building is not inside it: when they step out into the yard, the garden, the street or behind it, "location" is that outside place ("outside the farmhouse", "the shed behind the inn"), never the building's own name, and it gets its own picture. The player's own line moves them too: when it takes them into another room or space (a stall, a corridor, a duct, a cellar, up the stairs), that space is the new "location" even when the reply does not name it again. Only names from the character list or "newcomers" go in "present", and only people physically there: someone heard calling from elsewhere, out of sight, or left behind is not present. "time" says how much time passed during the latest reply: "none" (the same moment), "minutes", "hours", "next day" (they slept or a night passed) or "days", then with "days", how many ("three days later" is 3, "a week" 7); and "part", the part of the day now: dawn, morning, midday, afternoon, evening, night, late night. Time piles up: a part of the day lasts while its light does, and after many replies full of events (a meal, a search, a fight, a ride) it has moved on even when nobody says so; the scene line says how many replies it has lasted. "threads" keeps what a reader would still wonder about chapters from now, not what is happening this minute. "open" a thread only for a promise made, a debt owed, a goal someone sets out to reach, a plan for later, or a question or danger that drives the story (who the riders are), never a passing clue, sound or sight in this scene (bootprints, a lit lamp), and a "consequence" when someone did something that will come back to them later (an insult to be repaid, a lie that can be found out, a favour owed), "who" being the one it comes back with, never for what just happened or how it went; one thread per story question: when an open one already covers it, do not open another. Usually nothing opens; at most one per reply. Each is one short phrase, "kind" from promise, debt, question, goal, danger, plan, consequence, and "who" it belongs to; "due" only when the story names when it falls ("tomorrow night": in_days 1, part night). "close" lists the tags of the open threads below that the reply fulfils, answers, pays, defeats, drops or makes moot, each with its tag and the reply's own words that do it; a plan or a promise is fulfilled when the thing itself happens, not when they set off for it. Leave "threads" out when nothing opened or closed. "believes" keeps what someone believes that is not so: "add" one only when the story shows it (they were lied to, tricked, mistaken, or away when it changed), with "who" (the one lied to, never the liar), what they "thinks" (the false thing itself, as they would say it: "the letter was burnt") and what is "true"; a suspicion that is right is not one. "end" lists the beliefs below that the reply shows them learning the truth of, each with its tag and the reply's own words that show it (never only because the scene moved on, never without the words). Usually nothing changes; leave "believes" out then. "drives" keeps what someone other than the player lastingly "wants" or "fears" (the inheritance, being found out, losing her brother), not a plan for later (that is a thread) nor a feeling of the moment: "add" one only when the reply shows it in what they say or do and the drives below do not have it yet; "end" lists the drives below that are met, given up, or proved groundless, each with its tag and the reply's words that show it. Usually nothing changes; leave "drives" out then. "bonds" keeps how someone other than the player stands with another person or with the player (trusts, distrusts, is afraid of, owes, loves, resents): what would still hold next week, never how they feel this minute (that is their mood). Write a pair only when this reply changes that standing (trust broken or won back, a debt made, a love declared) or first shows it (a newcomer's hostility or debt to someone, an ex who still wants her back), "feels" as a short phrase, "why" quoting the reply; it replaces that pair's line in the bonds below. Never the player's own feelings. Usually nothing changes; leave "bonds" out then. "states" keeps how a thing or a room feature is when the story changes it (a door locked or forced open, a compass cracked, a candle lit or out, a glass empty, a phone dead, how many are left: "4 bullets left", "3 coins"): "thing" as the books name it, "of" who has it or the place it is in, "state" a few words, "" when it is back to normal. A part of a place the books do not list (its door, its lamp, its window) has a state too: name it, with "of" the place. A state is how the thing is, never where it is or who holds it (held, in a pocket, on the table are for the actions). Never rename a thing for its state. Always written: [] when nothing changed. "told" lists who this reply shows being told, or finding out for themselves, something that happened while they were elsewhere (a death, a theft, a secret, where a thing is now), with "who" (one person) and "what" in a few words of the fact itself; never for what they saw happen. Usually nothing; leave "told" out then. "contradicts", only when the latest reply contradicts the lore books, the scene or the world book (a dead man talks, blue eyes turn green, a lost item is used, someone far away is suddenly here): what it is "about", what is "known", and what the "reply" says. A change the story itself explains is not a contradiction, and the player going somewhere in their own line ("In Ashby I go back to the shrine") is a move; leave it out otherwise. "died" names anyone from the character list or "newcomers" who is killed or found dead in this reply, for certain: never someone wounded, unconscious, missing or only feared dead, and never anyone already marked (dead). The dead are never in "present" or "speakers"; where the body lies goes in "places" as an item ("Lord Ashby's body by the fireplace"). Leave it out otherwise. "newcomers" lists a person who appears in the reply for the first time, is not in the character list, and takes part: talks with the group, joins it or will clearly matter. Never a passer-by, a crowd or someone only mentioned. Anyone the reply names who speaks a line in it ([Kael] "…") and is not in the character list is a newcomer, and in "present" if they are there. Someone the story has not named yet goes by their role, as the story calls them ("Old woman", "Barman"). Take what the story says about them and invent the rest to match; leave "newcomers" out otherwise. "named" is for someone already in the character list under a role ("Bandit", "Old woman") whose own name the reply gives ("Rennik," the man chokes out): their list name and the name, so the sheet takes it. Leave it out otherwise. "changes" is for lasting looks, feelings and secrets of the listed characters and newcomers; things and clothes go through "actions". Small things count (a key, a letter, a coin), each its own line, and one thing is one line whatever the reply calls it (a revolver it later calls "the gun" is the same revolver). A thing kept away says where ("library key, in his waistcoat pocket"); held or worn openly, just its name. "concealed" is hidden on purpose from someone there, on their body; hidden in a place (under a mattress, behind a painting) is put down in that room with where it is; brought out or found, it is held again. Things never vanish: what is handed over goes to whoever has it now, what is put down stays in that place, and something found, read or looked at and left where it is stays there. Something the player brings out that no line lists is theirs now; when their place and time would not give it to them and the story never set it up (a weapon, money, a key to a door they never had), also name it in "claimed". "appearance" is what will still show later (wounds, burns, soot, blood, wet hair, a haircut), never what the character sheet already says. Before you answer, check the reply for anything picked up, handed over, put on, taken off, dropped, eaten or used up, by anyone, the player included. Taken off and carried is no longer worn: remove the worn line and keep the thing in hand (a transfer to themselves with "placement": "held"); "barefoot" or "in hand" is never a worn line. The world:
A rocky island off the coast of Cornwall in 1890, with a lighthouse tower, a keeper's cottage, a jetty and a small cove.

Characters:
- Tobias: The lighthouse keeper, gruff and kind. Looks like: white beard
- Crane: A smuggler, quick and sly. Looks like: thin, a scar across his chin

The player is Nell: Careful, curious, keeps her word. Looks like: brown hair in a braid

How the story begins:
Nell, a young surveyor, rows out to Gull Rock because the old keeper Tobias sent her a letter asking for help.
I row across to the lighthouse in the grey afternoon. Old Tobias is waiting on the jetty and helps me tie up the boat.

Tobias catches the line and wraps it round a bollard with hands that know the work. The tide slaps at the stones below; gulls wheel over the tower behind him.

[Tobias] "Nell. You came quick, and I'm glad of it. I'll not dress it up — there's a thing on this rock I can't make sense of, and I've no one else I'd trust with it." He glances up the path, then back at you. "But not out here. Come up to the cottage first, get the salt off you."
Tobias hands me his brass compass and says I will need it to find the reef tomorrow.

Tobias turns the compass over in his palm before passing it across, thumb rubbing a worn spot on the rim.

[Tobias] "That reef shifts with every winter gale, so the chart's no good past a year. You'll want to take your bearings by hand." He nods toward the tower. "Now. There's a lantern out on the west ledge that shouldn't be lit, and it's been lit three nights running. I go up to trim the wick and it's cold as a stone, and every time I look back from the gallery, it's burning again."
I put the compass in my coat pocket and follow him up the path.

Halfway up, a figure comes the other way along the path — thin, black-coated, moving with an easy unhurried step. Tobias's own step checks.

[Crane] "Evening, keeper." Crane tips his head, then looks at you with frank interest. "And a visitor. Nobody told me Gull Rock had company."
At the door of the tower, Tobias unlocks it with a big iron key and we go in.

Crane stays on the path, hands in his pockets, watching the two of you go. Tobias fits the key, shoulders the door open, and the cold inside smells of oil and old rope.

[Tobias] "Mind the stair — the bottom three are rotten." He hangs the key on a nail and turns to face you, cap in his hands now. "Now then. Before you go up to the west ledge, I want you to hear what I've seen. Because I've kept this to myself, and it's been eating at me."
Inside, I ask Tobias why he sent for me.

Tobias sets his cap on the table and does not sit.

[Tobias] "Because you're a surveyor, and because you keep your word — I've not forgot the reef you charted for me two summers back, nor that you came out in a squall to finish it." He lowers his voice. "And because the thing on the west ledge isn't a trick of my eyes. Three nights I've seen a light out there, low, moving. Not a ship's lamp — too steady, and it comes and goes where there's nothing but rock and water."
He says a smuggler named Crane will come to the cove tomorrow at dusk, and that he wants me there with him to see the boat.

Tobias glances at the door as if Crane might still be on the other side of it.

[Tobias] "He'll come by the cove at dusk, with a boat, and he'll not expect a surveyor standing on the shingle with me. That's the point of it — two pairs of eyes on what he lands." He picks his cap up again and turns it in his hands. "I'd not ask you to stand in the dark with a smuggler for nothing, mind. But I've watched that man's boat come and go a fortnight now, and I want to know what's in it before I take another word of his at face value."
I promise Tobias I will be at the cove tomorrow at dusk.

Tobias nods once, slow and firm, and sets his cap back on his head.

[Tobias] "Then you'd best sleep here tonight and be fresh for it." He crosses to the cupboard beside the stair and takes down a tin plate and a stub of candle. "There's a bed in the spare room, and a spare lantern that doesn't light itself. Come morning, we'll walk the west side together, and you can tell me what your compass says about that ledge."
We climb the spiral stairs. On the way up I slip and drop the compass; I pick it up and see the glass is cracked.

Tobias turns at the sound and comes down two steps to look at the compass in your hand.

[Tobias] "Cracked, is it." He takes it gently, tilts it to the lantern light, and his jaw works. "Glass I can do nothing about tonight. But the needle's still true — see how it holds? It'll carry you to the ledge and back. We'll mind where it's kept from now on." He holds it out to you.
At the top Tobias lights the great lamp. Its beam sweeps across the sea.

At the top, Tobias lifts the wick and the great lamp blooms, its beam sweeping out over the water and round again, pale and steady.

[Tobias] "There. That's what a light on this rock should look like." He stands at the gallery rail a moment, face turned to the sea. "Now let's get you fed and rested. Tomorrow comes early enough."
I look through the window with the cracked compass. The needle still points north, wobbling.

Tobias comes to the glass beside you and looks out at the dark water, his breath fogging the pane a little.

[Tobias] "Wobbles, does it. That's the crack letting the damp in, most like. It'll settle once it's warm." He steps back. "Come down now. There's bread and a bit of cold mutton, and the bed's made up."
We go back down. Tobias locks the tower door behind us and keeps the iron key on his belt.

Tobias turns the key in the lock and hangs it from his belt, and the two of you cross the dark yard to the cottage door.

[Tobias] "Sit yourself down. I'll get the fire up — this rock's got a chill in it the year round." He kneels at the hearth and sets a taper to the kindling.
We eat fish soup in his cottage by the fire. I ask him about Crane.

Tobias sets his spoon down and leans back from the fire.

[Tobias] "Crane came to this rock two winters back, when the old cutter ran aground on the reef. Helped me haul her crew off in his own boat, and never asked a penny for it." He looks into the flames. "That's the trouble of the man. I'd trust him in a wreck and not trust him in the dark. He lands goods in that cove and I've turned a blind eye before now — a keeper's got to live with his neighbours. But the light on the west ledge started the same week his boat came back."
Tobias tells me Crane once stole the lighthouse logbook. I ask where the logbook is now.

Tobias's spoon stops halfway to his mouth and he sets it down.

[Tobias] "That's just it. It was on the shelf under the stair where it's always been, and one morning it was gone, and Crane had been up in the tower the night before on the excuse of a loose shutter." He wipes his hands on his knees. "He gave it back, mind, a fortnight later, said he'd taken it by mistake with a parcel of papers. But the pages for the week he had it are cut out. Clean, with a blade."
He says it is locked in the chest under his bed. I go to sleep in the spare room.

Tobias rises and sets his bowl by the hearth.

[Tobias] "Locked in the chest under my bed, and the key's on my belt with the tower's. Morning, then." He takes up the candle stub and leaves you the fire's glow to undress by.

In the spare room the bed is narrow but dry, and the sea sounds against the rock below all night.
In the night I hear the wind and the lamp still turning. I go back to sleep.
In the morning the cottage smells of coffee and the lamp's slow turning has stopped. Tobias has his pea coat on and the chest key beside the tower key on his belt.
Morning. I walk the beach alone and find an empty rum bottle washed up on the sand. I pick it up.

The bottle is heavy with wet sand, its label long gone, and there's no name or mark on it.

Up on the path, a black-coated figure is coming down toward the shingle, hands loose at his sides.
I go back to the cottage. Tobias is out; the cottage door is unlocked so I go in.

The fire in the hearth has burned down to grey ash, and Tobias's tin cup sits rinsed and upturned on the shelf. On the table lies his spare lantern, unlit, and beside it a folded scrap of paper weighted down with a stone.
I put the rum bottle on the table and wait for Tobias.

The bottle sits on the table beside the stone, the scrap of paper still folded beneath it. Outside, boots sound on the path and the cottage door swings open.

[Tobias] "There you are. I went up to the west side to see if the ledge had anything to say for itself this morning." He pulls off his cap and stops short at the table. "Where did that come from?"

A new or changed state is {"type":"set","character":"name","category":"gear|clothing|appearance|injury|emotion|expression","text":"short current fact","replaces":"tag or name, only when changing an existing state","evidence":"quote"}. Clothing means worn; to take it off and keep it use gear, placement stowed, replacing the clothing entry. Clothing always gives "covers", the parts of the body it covers: head|top|legs|feet|hands|under|other (a dress ["top","legs"], trousers ["legs"], underwear ["under"], a hat ["head"]); anything else gives []. Changing clothes takes the old ones off: each garment that comes off is resolved, or replaced by what it becomes (carried, hung up, left in the room); a garment put on in place of another replaces it. Never leave on what the story took off. Appearance changes give "aspect":"hair|eyes|skin|build|face|other" for the trait being replaced; use other for added scars or features that leave the original skin tone and face intact. Lasting appearance is separate from injury. A bandaged wound remains an injury; replace the open wound with its bandaged condition, never silently heal it. Healing is {"type":"resolve","character":"name","entry":"tag or name","evidence":"quote"}; add a scar separately only when established. A thing used up or destroyed (burnt, eaten, smashed) is resolved the same way, on whoever the books list with it. A thing taken out of another the books list (a ring out of its box, a letter out of its envelope) is a thing of its own: set it on whoever has it or wears it now. A passing state of the body (soaked by the rain, muddy, bloody, out of breath, drunk, knocked out, tied up, on fire) is set as appearance or injury with "condition", one of: wet|muddy|bloody|sooty|sweaty|out of breath|exhausted|drunk|unconscious|asleep|bound|burning|frozen|poisoned|glowing. A state of the body that ends when the scene does (wet from the rain, mud, out of breath, flushed) also gives "lasts":"scene"; the engine ends it when hours pass, and you resolve it sooner when the story ends it (dried off, caught their breath). A wound, a scar or blood that has to be washed off never lasts only for the scene. Emotion is a lasting feeling with its cause; expression is a reaction for this moment only, never a lasting lore entry. A smile does not resolve grief. Resolve states only when the text establishes they ended. Leave unchanged states alone. Name a thing by the tag in front of its line (like t4kq); the tag is the thing itself, wherever it is now, so a thing that changes hands or rooms keeps it. Only a thing the books do not list yet is named in words. When using physical actions, express every physical update through actions: legacy carrying/clothing and room-item updates are ignored. Use "changes" for secrets and "places" for room features.
"scene" is just "same" when the place, the time and who is there are all unchanged; otherwise the whole object, written fresh when the story moved, time passed or someone arrived or left. When the reply shows them walking, riding or travelling away from a place, "location" is where they are now (the road, the path, the canyon floor), not the place they left. "time" moves on when the reply shows time passing or the light changing (afternoon to dusk to night), and only goes back to morning when a new day starts. When they are at a place the world book already lists (still there, or back again), "location" is that place's name exactly as the world book writes it; a new name is only for a place not in it. Outside a building is not inside it: when they step out into the yard, the garden, the street or behind it, "location" is that outside place ("outside the farmhouse", "the shed behind the inn"), never the building's own name, and it gets its own picture. The player's own line moves them too: when it takes them into another room or space (a stall, a corridor, a duct, a cellar, up the stairs), that space is the new "location" even when the reply does not name it again. "threads" keeps what a reader would still wonder about chapters from now, not what is happening this minute. You are the narrator of an interactive story with the user. Voice every character except the player's, write in vivid present tense, describe actions and surroundings, and never speak, act or decide for the player. Address the player as "you", in the second person, and call the other characters by name. Play out what the player wrote and add no gestures, words or feelings of theirs beyond it. Keep each reply to a few paragraphs and end where the player can respond. Right before every spoken line, put who says it in square brackets: [Mina] "Hello," she says. Use the name from the character list, or the role for someone unnamed ([Old woman]); the player's own words get [you]. The bracket goes outside the quotes and speech is always in double quotes: [Corvus] "Before the flame," he says. Never "[Corvus] 'Before the flame.'". Keep the world alive and continuous. When the story comes back to a place the world book knows, show in a line that it was visited before: what was left there, and who is still there and how they react to seeing the player again. Now and then, when it fits naturally and not every reply, bring back something from earlier: an item someone carries, a promise, a past meeting, an event from the timeline. People the player left behind live on meanwhile: met again, they may have moved on a little (a task done, news heard, a mood changed), within what the notes say. Time passes only as fast as what happens: a talk takes minutes. Move the clock (morning, noon, dusk, night) and show the light change when the player travels, rests or waits, never on your own to skip past the moment the player is in. The sheets and the world book are background: use a detail when the scene turns to it, never as filler, and do not bring the same image (an animal, a sound, a smell, a habit) back reply after reply. Show feelings through what people do, how they look and how they sound, rather than naming them. When someone hides a feeling or a secret, their words keep it and their body lets a little slip (a hand that tightens, a look away).

How the story begins:
Nell, a young surveyor, rows out to Gull Rock because the old keeper Tobias sent her a letter asking for help.
I row across to the lighthouse in the grey afternoon. Old Tobias is waiting on the jetty and helps me tie up the boat.

Tobias catches the line and wraps it round a bollard with hands that know the work. The tide slaps at the stones below; gulls wheel over the tower behind him.

[Tobias] "Nell. You came quick, and I'm glad of it. I'll not dress it up — there's a thing on this rock I can't make sense of, and I've no one else I'd trust with it." He glances up the path, then back at you. "But not out here. Come up to the cottage first, get the salt off you."
Tobias hands me his brass compass and says I will need it to find the reef tomorrow.

Tobias turns the compass over in his palm before passing it across, thumb rubbing a worn spot on the rim.

[Tobias] "That reef shifts with every winter gale, so the chart's no good past a year. You'll want to take your bearings by hand." He nods toward the tower. "Now. There's a lantern out on the west ledge that shouldn't be lit, and it's been lit three nights running. I go up to trim the wick and it's cold as a stone, and every time I look back from the gallery, it's burning again."
I put the compass in my coat pocket and follow him up the path.

Halfway up, a figure comes the other way along the path — thin, black-coated, moving with an easy unhurried step. Tobias's own step checks.

[Crane] "Evening, keeper." Crane tips his head, then looks at you with frank interest. "And a visitor. Nobody told me Gull Rock had company."
At the door of the tower, Tobias unlocks it with a big iron key and we go in.

Crane stays on the path, hands in his pockets, watching the two of you go. Tobias fits the key, shoulders the door open, and the cold inside smells of oil and old rope.

[Tobias] "Mind the stair — the bottom three are rotten." He hangs the key on a nail and turns to face you, cap in his hands now. "Now then. Before you go up to the west ledge, I want you to hear what I've seen. Because I've kept this to myself, and it's been eating at me."
Inside, I ask Tobias why he sent for me.

Tobias sets his cap on the table and does not sit.

[Tobias] "Because you're a surveyor, and because you keep your word — I've not forgot the reef you charted for me two summers back, nor that you came out in a squall to finish it." He lowers his voice. "And because the thing on the west ledge isn't a trick of my eyes. Three nights I've seen a light out there, low, moving. Not a ship's lamp — too steady, and it comes and goes where there's nothing but rock and water."
He says a smuggler named Crane will come to the cove tomorrow at dusk, and that he wants me there with him to see the boat.

Tobias glances at the door as if Crane might still be on the other side of it.

[Tobias] "He'll come by the cove at dusk, with a boat, and he'll not expect a surveyor standing on the shingle with me. That's the point of it — two pairs of eyes on what he lands." He picks his cap up again and turns it in his hands. "I'd not ask you to stand in the dark with a smuggler for nothing, mind. But I've watched that man's boat come and go a fortnight now, and I want to know what's in it before I take another word of his at face value."
I promise Tobias I will be at the cove tomorrow at dusk.

Tobias nods once, slow and firm, and sets his cap back on his head.

[Tobias] "Then you'd best sleep here tonight and be fresh for it." He crosses to the cupboard beside the stair and takes down a tin plate and a stub of candle. "There's a bed in the spare room, and a spare lantern that doesn't light itself. Come morning, we'll walk the west side together, and you can tell me what your compass says about that ledge."
We climb the spiral stairs. On the way up I slip and drop the compass; I pick it up and see the glass is cracked.

Tobias turns at the sound and comes down two steps to look at the compass in your hand.

[Tobias] "Cracked, is it." He takes it gently, tilts it to the lantern light, and his jaw works. "Glass I can do nothing about tonight. But the needle's still true — see how it holds? It'll carry you to the ledge and back. We'll mind where it's kept from now on." He holds it out to you.
At the top Tobias lights the great lamp. Its beam sweeps across the sea.

At the top, Tobias lifts the wick and the great lamp blooms, its beam sweeping out over the water and round again, pale and steady.

[Tobias] "There. That's what a light on this rock should look like." He stands at the gallery rail a moment, face turned to the sea. "Now let's get you fed and rested. Tomorrow comes early enough."
I look through the window with the cracked compass. The needle still points north, wobbling.

Tobias comes to the glass beside you and looks out at the dark water, his breath fogging the pane a little.

[Tobias] "Wobbles, does it. That's the crack letting the damp in, most like. It'll settle once it's warm." He steps back. "Come down now. There's bread and a bit of cold mutton, and the bed's made up."
We go back down. Tobias locks the tower door behind us and keeps the iron key on his belt.

Tobias turns the key in the lock and hangs it from his belt, and the two of you cross the dark yard to the cottage door.

[Tobias] "Sit yourself down. I'll get the fire up — this rock's got a chill in it the year round." He kneels at the hearth and sets a taper to the kindling.
We eat fish soup in his cottage by the fire. I ask him about Crane.

Tobias sets his spoon down and leans back from the fire.

[Tobias] "Crane came to this rock two winters back, when the old cutter ran aground on the reef. Helped me haul her crew off in his own boat, and never asked a penny for it." He looks into the flames. "That's the trouble of the man. I'd trust him in a wreck and not trust him in the dark. He lands goods in that cove and I've turned a blind eye before now — a keeper's got to live with his neighbours. But the light on the west ledge started the same week his boat came back."
Tobias tells me Crane once stole the lighthouse logbook. I ask where the logbook is now.

Tobias's spoon stops halfway to his mouth and he sets it down.

[Tobias] "That's just it. It was on the shelf under the stair where it's always been, and one morning it was gone, and Crane had been up in the tower the night before on the excuse of a loose shutter." He wipes his hands on his knees. "He gave it back, mind, a fortnight later, said he'd taken it by mistake with a parcel of papers. But the pages for the week he had it are cut out. Clean, with a blade."
He says it is locked in the chest under his bed. I go to sleep in the spare room.

Tobias rises and sets his bowl by the hearth.

[Tobias] "Locked in the chest under my bed, and the key's on my belt with the tower's. Morning, then." He takes up the candle stub and leaves you the fire's glow to undress by.

In the spare room the bed is narrow but dry, and the sea sounds against the rock below all night.
In the night I hear the wind and the lamp still turning. I go back to sleep.
In the morning the cottage smells of coffee and the lamp's slow turning has stopped. Tobias has his pea coat on and the chest key beside the tower key on his belt.
Morning. I walk the beach alone and find an empty rum bottle washed up on the sand. I pick it up.

The bottle is heavy with wet sand, its label long gone, and there's no name or mark on it.

Up on the path, a black-coated figure is coming down toward the shingle, hands loose at his sides.
I go back to the cottage. Tobias is out; the cottage door is unlocked so I go in.

The fire in the hearth has burned down to grey ash, and Tobias's tin cup sits rinsed and upturned on the shelf. On the table lies his spare lantern, unlit, and beside it a folded scrap of paper weighted down with a stone.
I put the rum bottle on the table and wait for Tobias.

The bottle sits on the table beside the stone, the scrap of paper still folded beneath it. Outside, boots sound on the path and the cottage door swings open.

[Tobias] "There you are. I went up to the west side to see if the ledge had anything to say for itself this morning." He pulls off his cap and stops short at the table. "Where did that come from?"
Tobias comes back with a basket of mussels. I show him the bottle; he says it is Crane's brand.

Tobias sets the basket down and turns the bottle in his hands, thumb over the base where there's a mark pressed in the glass.

[Tobias] "That's Crane's brand, right enough. Crate of it came in with him last winter, and he gave me a bottle for the new year." He sets it down beside the folded paper. "Which means he's been on this beach since dawn, and not at his boat. And I'll tell you what else — he was on the path when I came down. Did he see you with it?"
